title: "Fixed it."
author: Jenny Allen
summary: Jenny Allen recounts walking into a senior leadership meeting without a deliverable—because she could find no evidence that the problem they'd asked her to fix was the actual problem. The leadership team had seen poor employee survey scores in 'leadership communication,' immediately concluded that managers needed training, and tasked her with developing it. Allen's refusal to execute without a diagnosis forced a productive pause that led to a cross-functional investigation into the real root cause. The piece is a first-person argument against the human tendency to move from problem identification to plausible solution without pausing to test the diagnosis—a pattern Allen observed again and again in organizational life, where training became the reflexive answer to virtually every people problem.
points: Leaders routinely mistake 'most visible cause' for 'actual cause,' jumping to intervention before testing whether they've correctly diagnosed the problem.

Training is identified as the organizational equivalent of a catch-all solution—applied to leadership presence, communication failures, and accountability gaps before any of the root causes have been verified.
Allen's willingness to walk into an executive meeting with a question instead of a deliverable—at professional risk—modeled the disciplined skepticism she argues all change agents should practice.
The piece captures a key organizational dynamic: leadership teams under pressure move from uncertainty to action as quickly as possible, because action feels more competent than continued inquiry.
The practical rule derived: question the diagnosis before deciding on a treatment—a principle as applicable to management as it is to medicine.
quotes: All I had was a question: Why do we think the managers are the problem?
She realized they'd done what harried leadership teams often do—saw a problem, latched onto a plausible explanation, and moved to solve it without testing the assumption.
Training was the catch-all solution to just about every organizational ill—usually before anyone had fully examined the issue.

When a problem arises, people naturally reach for the most visible cause so they can quickly move from uncertainty to action. Then they can declare it handled without uncovering any deeper, decidedly more inconvenient realities.
All the time and money in the world won't help you if you're solving the wrong problem or targeting the wrong cause.
I went into that leadership meeting fully expecting a smackdown. I came out with a rule I used for the rest of my career: question the diagnosis before deciding on a treatment.
